title: Gulf Stock Markets Rise as Strong Earnings Offset Stalled Iran Talks
excerpt: Saudi Arabia's Tadawul led regional gains on Sunday despite no progress in peace negotiations and continued disruptions to Strait of Hormuz shipping traffic.
body:
• Saudi Arabia's Tadawul index rose 0.9% to 10,920, led by Al Rajhi Bank (+1.5%) and Saudi Aramco (+1%), while Qatar's index gained 0.2% and Egypt's benchmark added 1.1%.
  • Gulf stock markets advanced despite stalled U.S.-Iran peace talks, with Iran urging Washington to concede defeat and Trump warning Americans of persistently high fuel prices.
  • Oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has yet to fully resume, with recent data showing just six vessels transiting daily versus a pre-conflict average of 125 to 140.
  • Brent crude settled at $88.52 per barrel, up 1.67%, as supply disruptions in the Gulf continued to support elevated oil prices.

Most Gulf stock markets posted gains on Sunday despite ongoing uncertainty in the region, as resilient corporate earnings and elevated oil prices outweighed the absence of progress in peace negotiations between Washington and Tehran.

Saudi Arabia's benchmark Tadawul All Share Index advanced 0.9% to 10,920, with banking heavyweight Al Rajhi Bank climbing 1.5% and oil major Saudi Aramco adding 1%. Qatar's index edged up 0.2% to 10,045, boosted by a 1.5% gain in Qatar National Bank, the Gulf's largest lender.

Geopolitical Standoff Deepens

The gains came against a backdrop of deteriorating diplomatic signals. Iran urged the United States on Saturday to concede defeat, while President Donald Trump branded Tehran "very evil" and warned Americans to brace for persistently high fuel prices because of the conflict.

The exchange of rhetoric underscored the absence of meaningful progress in negotiations aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the critical waterway that handled roughly one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before Iran's blockade following U.S. and Israeli strikes in late February.

"Gulf equities are gaining support from resilient bank earnings, strong non-oil growth, healthy oil prices, and hopes of easier U.S. monetary policy. However, it is still too early to call this a sustained bull market."

— Rania Gule, Senior Market Analyst, XS.com – MENA

Iran and Oman had reportedly reached agreement on coordinates for a new shipping route through the strait, but Tehran has conditioned any reopening on the United States meeting further demands, including compensation for strikes on Iranian territory and the release of frozen assets.

Shipping Traffic Remains a Fraction of Normal

Data from earlier in the week showed just six vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz on a single day, compared with a 10-day average of about 11 — itself a tiny fraction of the 125 to 140 daily transits seen before the conflict. The bottleneck has sustained upward pressure on oil prices, with Brent crude futures settling at $88.52 per barrel on Friday, up $1.45 or 1.67%.

The shipping disruption has also widened beyond the Hormuz chokepoint. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have launched missile attacks on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, and the UAE's Abu Dhabi National Oil Company said 15 of its vessels had been attacked while transiting the strait since the conflict began.

Earnings and Oil Underpin Markets

Analysts pointed to several factors supporting Gulf equities despite the geopolitical overhang. Saudi Aramco's second-quarter net profit surged 44% year-over-year to $32.69 billion, reflecting the impact of elevated crude prices. Strong non-oil economic growth across the Gulf Cooperation Council states, particularly in Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030-driven diversification sectors, has also bolstered investor confidence.

In corporate news, Tihama for Advertising rose 7.3% after its board terminated CEO Hussain Masoud Al-Dossari's contract and named Shakir Ahmed Saleh Al-Saleh as his replacement.

Outside the Gulf, Egypt's blue-chip EGX30 index advanced 1.1% to 55,855, with Telecom Egypt climbing 3.6% on the back of a steep rise in quarterly profit. Bahrain dipped 0.1%, while Oman added 0.3% and Kuwait traded flat.

What's Next

Investor attention this week will remain fixed on any developments in the Iran-Oman shipping lane framework and the broader question of whether Tehran and Washington can find common ground. A lasting market uptrend will depend on continued foreign inflows, solid earnings momentum, stronger trading volumes, and some measure of geopolitical stability — conditions that remain elusive in the current environment. Until the Hormuz situation is resolved, oil prices and Gulf equity markets will likely continue to trade on the tension between strong fundamentals and elevated risk.
nri_angle: Elevated oil prices driven by the Hormuz disruption affect energy costs globally, while Gulf market performance reflects the economic resilience of a region home to significant Indian and South Asian expatriate communities.
